# Linear Mixed Effect Models I

> Learning Objectives
>
> By the end of this lecture, you should be able to:
>
> 1. Understand the difference between **fixed effects** and **random effects**
> 2. Recognize **clustered** and **longitudinal** data structures
> 3. Formulate **linear mixed models mathematically**
> 4. Implement LMM in **SAS using PROC MIXED**
> 5. Interpret model outputs

## Introduction

In previous lectures, we studied linear regression models of the form:

$$
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i + \epsilon_i, \quad \epsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2)
$$

A key assumption is:

> Observations are **independent**

However, this assumption often fails in real applications.

::: {.callout-example title = "Clustered Data"}

- Students within schools
- Patients within hospitals

Observations within the same group tend to be **similar**, leading to:

$$
\text{Corr}(Y_{ij}, Y_{ik}) \neq 0
$$

:::


::: {.callout-example title = "Longitudinal Data"}

Repeated measurements on the same subject

Example 

- Measuring performance across trials

This leads to:

$$
Y_{i1}, Y_{i2}, \dots, Y_{iT} \text{ are correlated}
$$

:::

This can be written as the additive structure of the **fixed effects** and **random effects**.

::: {.callout-definition title = "Fixed vs Random Effects"}

**Fixed Effects**

- Parameters associated with **entire population**
- Example:

$$
\beta_1 = \text{effect of treatment}
$$


**Random Effects**

- Capture **subject-specific variation**

Let:

$$
u_i \sim N(0, \sigma_u^2)
$$

Then each subject has its own deviation.

:::

This can be modelled using something called Linear Mixed 

## Linear Mixed Effect Model (LMEM)

A general LMEM is:

$$
Y_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{ij} + u_i + \epsilon_{ij},
$$

where

- $u_i \sim N(0, \sigma_u^2)$ (random effect)
- $\epsilon_{ij} \sim N(0, \sigma^2)$ (residual)

**Interpretation**

- $\beta_0, \beta_1$: fixed effects
- $u_i$: subject-specific deviation
- $Y_{ij}$ are correlated because of shared $u_i$

## Variance Structure

We can derive:

$$
\text{Var}(Y_{ij}) = \sigma_u^2 + \sigma^2
$$

$$
\text{Cov}(Y_{ij}, Y_{ik}) = \sigma_u^2
$$

Thus:

$$
\text{Corr}(Y_{ij}, Y_{ik}) = \frac{\sigma_u^2}{\sigma_u^2 + \sigma^2}
$$


## Example Dataset

``` r
DATA performance;
    INPUT id $ age group $ trial score;
    DATALINES;
SY 34 A 1 14.3
SY 34 A 2 21.4
SY 34 A 3 27.6
SY 34 A 4 31.1
SY 34 A 5 33.2
WL 33 A 1 13.2
WL 33 A 2 21.4
WL 33 A 3 23.3
WL 33 A 4 30.0
WL 33 A 5 38.6
ZN 43 B 1 15.9
ZN 43 B 2 23.4
ZN 43 B 3 22.0
ZN 43 B 4 29.0
ZN 43 B 5 33.6
;
RUN;
```

**Step 1: Incorrect Model (Ignoring Correlation)**

```r
PROC REG DATA=performance;
    MODEL score = trial;
RUN;
```

Problem:

- Assumes independence
- Underestimates variance


**Step 2: Random Intercept Model**

``` r
PROC MIXED DATA=performance;
    CLASS id;
    MODEL score = trial;
    RANDOM INTERCEPT / SUBJECT=id;
RUN;
```

Model:

$$
Y_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot trial_{ij} + u_i + \epsilon_{ij}
$$


**Step 3: Add Fixed Effects**

```r 
PROC MIXED DATA=performance;
    CLASS id group;
    MODEL score = trial group;
    RANDOM INTERCEPT / SUBJECT=id;
RUN;
```

Model:

$$
Y_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 trial_{ij} + \beta_2 group_i + u_i + \epsilon_{ij}
$$


**Step 4: Random Slope Model**

```sas
PROC MIXED DATA=performance;
    CLASS id;
    MODEL score = trial;
    RANDOM INTERCEPT trial / SUBJECT=id;
RUN;
```

Model:

$$
Y_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 trial_{ij} + u_{0i} + u_{1i} trial_{ij} + \epsilon_{ij}
$$


## Conceptual Visualization

- Regression: one line
- Mixed model: multiple lines (one per subject)


## In-Class Questions

::: {.callout-exercise}

Which variable is most appropriate as a random effect?

(A) trial  
(B) score  
(C) id  
(D) group  

:::

::: {.callout-exercise}

Why include random effects?

(A) Increase sample size  
(B) Model dependence  
(C) Remove variables  
(D) Normalize data  

:::

::: {.callout-exercise}

Ignoring clustering leads to:

(A) Correct inference  
(B) Smaller errors  
(C) Incorrect standard errors  
(D) Better prediction  

:::

::: {.callout-note title = "Key Takeaways"}

- Mixed models handle **correlated data**
- Random effects introduce **dependence structure**
- Important for:
  - Longitudinal data
  - Clustered data
- Implemented via `PROC MIXED` in SAS

:::
